Maladaptive Strategies.value: I force myself to think only positive thoughts
Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).
Any form of physical contact with others

Negative Appraisals.value: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened

issues.item: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: The appraisal of feared uncontrollable rage is not well supported by the rest of the profile. There are no corresponding trigger, threat, memory, or strategy items suggesting anger-driven reactivity, aggression risk, or conflict; the other appraisals instead center on shame and hopelessness after rape. This makes the rage item clinically discordant within the selected five components.

issues.item: Constant Socialising: I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts
issues.explanation: The strategy of constant socialising is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile in this rape-related presentation. The selected triggers are solitary/sensory reminders (silence, outdoor smells, anniversary), and the appraisals are shame, suicidality, and feared rage. Constantly surrounding oneself with people does not connect clearly to these reminders and is somewhat at odds with body shame after rape, making it the least coherent avoidance/coping item here.

vignette:
Martha was seventy-four years old and had worked the soil of the Central Valley for more than four decades. She had been born in a small village in Ghana and had come to America in her twenties, carrying little more than a belief in hard work and the memory of red earth after rain. For most of her life, the smell of turned earth had meant something good-it meant planting, it meant harvest, it meant the slow reliable rhythm of seasons. But that had changed two years ago, on a late October evening when she had stayed behind to finish a row of tomatoes while the others packed up. The man who found her in the dark was someone she knew from the next farm over, someone who had smiled at her at the market. She had not screamed because there was no one left to hear her, and the silence that settled after he was gone was worse than anything she had ever heard. It was a thick, living silence, the kind that seemed to press into her ears and stay there.

In the weeks that followed, Martha did not tell anyone. She told herself that if she just thought about good things-her grandchildren, the wedding she had attended last spring, the way her partner Joseph made tea for her in the morning-then the memory would shrink and fade. She forced herself to smile when Joseph asked about her day. She forced herself to say she was fine. But the positive thoughts felt thin and brittle, like paper laid over a hole, and the hole only grew. By the time the anniversary of the event came around, she found herself unable to leave the house. She told Joseph she had a stomach bug, and she lay in bed with the curtains drawn, listening to the silence that now lived inside her.

The smell of soil became unbearable. She began to avoid the fields entirely, calling in sick, then taking unpaid leave, then finally telling the farm supervisor that her back was too old for the work. Joseph did not understand why she stopped gardening, why she no longer walked out to the small plot behind their trailer where she had always grown okra and collard greens. She could not explain it to him. She could not explain that the smell of damp earth made her feel as though the event was happening again, as though the dirt beneath her fingernails was the dirt from that evening. She began showering three times a day, sometimes four, scrubbing her skin until it was raw. She felt dirty in a way that no amount of soap could reach. She felt ashamed of her own body, of what had been done to it, of the fact that she had not fought harder, had not screamed louder, had not done something different.

Physical contact became impossible. When Joseph reached for her hand at the dinner table, she flinched. When he tried to hug her, she went rigid. She saw the hurt in his eyes, but what frightened her more was the feeling of his skin against hers-it made her stomach turn, made her feel as though she was being touched by the man from the farm all over again. She began sleeping on the couch. She began eating alone. She stopped going to church, because the silence during prayer was the same kind of silence that had followed the event, and she could not bear to sit in it.

By the time she came to the clinic, she had lost nearly fifteen pounds and had not worked in six months. Her PCL-5 score was sixty-five. She told the clinician, in a voice so quiet it was almost a whisper, that she was not sure her life was worth living anymore. She said she felt like a contaminated thing, like something spoiled that could not be cleaned. She said she knew she was supposed to think positively, and she had tried, but the positive thoughts felt like lies. What she hoped for, she said, was to feel clean again. What she feared was that she never would.
